title: Proportional Action in PID Control
body:
Proportional Action in PID Control is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats proportional action in pid control as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Proportional action is the foundation of classical PID control: the control signal is proportional to the present error, so a larger tilt of the balancing robot draws a stronger correcting torque. It acts immediately, with no memory and no prediction, which makes it the easiest term to understand, analyse, and trust. Its gain, Kp, sets how aggressively the controller reacts, and choosing Kp is the first decision in any PID tuning task.

Proportional action alone cannot finish the job. A proportional-only controller leaves a steady-state error whenever a constant disturbance, such as a slope or an off-centre load, must be opposed, because the correcting torque vanishes exactly when the error vanishes. It also cannot anticipate motion, so a fast-moving robot can overshoot before the proportional term reacts. These limits are why the integral and derivative terms exist, and why proportional action is best read as one member of a team rather than a complete controller.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for proportional action in pid control. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. The output reads: error 0.05 proportional output 1.5; error 0.1 proportional output 3.0; error 0.2 proportional output 6.0; error -0.1 proportional output -3.0 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

In the balancing-robot model used across this database, the error is defined as the negative of the tilt angle, so a positive tilt produces a negative, restoring control signal. The demo computes the proportional output for four errors at the edition gain, showing the strict linear relationship between error and output. Linearity is the source of both the strength and the weakness of this term: it is exactly predictable, and exactly unable to adapt when the plant changes.

title: Integral Action in PID Control
body:
Integral Action in PID Control is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. It treats integral action in pid control as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Integral action accumulates the error over time, so a small but persistent tilt eventually produces a large correcting signal. This is what removes steady-state error: where proportional action alone would settle with a constant offset under a constant disturbance, the integral term keeps growing until the offset is driven out. It is the controller's memory, and it is the reason PID can hold a robot upright on a gentle slope once it has had time to learn the required holding torque.

Memory has costs. An integral term that accumulates during a large transient can overshoot badly when the error changes sign, a phenomenon called windup, and it reacts slowly because it must wait for error to accumulate. Practical implementations therefore clamp the integral, pause it while the actuator is saturated, or both. The demo shows the accumulation step by step for a constant error, making visible the mechanism that both removes steady-state error and demands anti-windup care.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. title: Derivative Action in PID Control
body:
Derivative Action in PID Control is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats derivative action in pid control as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Derivative action responds to the rate of change of the error, not to the error itself. When the balancing robot is falling toward upright, the derivative term already opposes the motion, adding damping that prevents overshoot; when the robot is moving away from upright, it adds to the restoring effort. It is the controller's prediction, estimated from the current trend, and it is what lets a well-tuned PID settle quickly without oscillation.

Prediction from a single difference is fragile. Sensor noise is amplified by differentiation, so a noisy tilt measurement produces a jittery derivative term, and practical controllers filter the derivative or compute it from a smoothed signal. Derivative action also contributes nothing at rest, so it cannot hold a robot against a constant disturbance on its own. The demo computes the derivative contribution for four angular rates, showing the clean linear damping law that real implementations must protect from noise.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for derivative action in pid control. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. The output reads: angular rate 0.0 derivative output -0.0; angular rate 0.5 derivative output -4.0; angular rate -0.5 derivative output 4.0; angular rate 1.0 derivative output -8.0; derivative output opposes motion, adding damping before overshoot occurs Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

In this database the error is the negative of the tilt, so the derivative of the error is the negative of the angular rate, and the derivative output is the gain times that negative rate. The sign convention matters: the term must oppose motion, not assist it, and a sign error here turns damping into excitation. title: PID Tuning Methods
body:
PID Tuning Methods is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats pid tuning methods as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Tuning is the procedure that turns the PID structure into a working controller for a particular plant. The classical Ziegler-Nichols method raises the proportional gain until the loop oscillates steadily, records that ultimate gain Ku and ultimate period Tu, and then derives all three gains from fixed formulas. Model-based tuning instead identifies a plant model first and computes gains that place the closed-loop poles at chosen locations. Both routes share one property: their result is a set of numbers fitted to one plant, measured or modelled at tuning time.

That fitted-to-one-plant property is the hinge of this whole database. A tuning method is a contract with the physics present during tuning; when the physics change, the contract must be renegotiated by retuning. Good practice therefore records the tuning conditions alongside the gains, validates the tuned loop against disturbances, and schedules re-tuning whenever the plant is modified. The demo applies the Ziegler-Nichols formulas to one ultimate gain and period, showing how a single oscillation experiment determines a complete gain set.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for pid tuning methods. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. title: Neural Network Controller Fundamentals
body:
Neural Network Controller Fundamentals is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats neural network controller fundamentals as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

A neural network controller replaces the fixed PID formula with a learned mapping from measured state to control signal. In the simplest form used here, the tilt angle and angular rate feed a hidden unit with a saturating activation, and the hidden unit's output is scaled into a control torque. The weights of that mapping are not derived from a plant model; they are learned from experience, by adjusting them until the robot balances across the conditions it encounters.

The learned mapping has two properties that matter for this comparison. First, it is nonlinear: the saturating activation lets the controller respond differently in different regions of the state space, which a linear PID cannot do. Second, it is fitted to the distribution of conditions seen during learning, not to a single plant model, so its behaviour under new conditions depends on how broadly it was trained. The demo runs one hidden unit over three states, showing how tilt and rate combine into a bounded control signal.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for neural network controller fundamentals. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. The output reads: theta 0.12 omega 0.0 hidden -0.9737 control -5.8425; theta 0.05 omega 0.3 hidden -0.9705 control -5.8227; theta -0.08 omega -0.2 hidden 0.9776 control 5.8655 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

The demo's weights are illustrative, chosen so the control signal opposes the tilt in each case, and the output is bounded by the saturation of the activation function. Boundedness is a practical virtue: a saturating controller cannot demand an unbounded torque from a finite actuator. It is also a limit: once saturated, the controller cannot distinguish a large error from a larger one, which is one reason hybrid designs keep a linear loop underneath the learned layer.

title: Online Learning and Adaptation Mechanisms
body:
Online Learning and Adaptation Mechanisms is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats online learning and adaptation mechanisms as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Online learning is what separates an adaptive controller from a merely learned one. Instead of freezing the weights after training, an adaptive controller keeps updating them while the robot runs, using each new measurement as one more training example. When the plant changes, the persistent error drives the weights toward values that cancel the new behaviour, without any engineer intervening to retune. Adaptation is therefore not a feature added to the controller; it is the controller's normal operation extended into deployment.

The update rule in the demo is gradient descent on the control error: the weight moves in proportion to the error and to the input that caused it, scaled by a learning rate. The learning rate is the adaptation analogue of a PID gain, and it carries the same trade-off: too small and adaptation is too slow to help, too large and the weights oscillate or diverge. Stability of the learning loop, not just of the control loop, must therefore be established, which is why adaptive control theory pairs every update rule with a convergence argument.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for online learning and adaptation mechanisms. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. title: The Balancing Robot Setup
body:
The Balancing Robot Setup is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats the balancing robot setup as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

The balancing robot in this database is modelled as an inverted pendulum: a mass balanced above a pivot, with gravity pulling any tilt further from upright. The upright position is an unstable equilibrium, so without control even a tiny initial tilt grows, slowly at first and then rapidly. The control problem is to apply torque at the pivot, or equivalently to move the base, so that the tilt is driven back toward zero faster than gravity drives it away.

The model used in the demos is deliberately simple: angular acceleration equals gravity's overturning term, plus the applied control torque scaled by actuator effectiveness, minus a small friction term, plus any external disturbance torque. Its parameters stand for the robot's real properties: the gravity term encodes the pendulum length and mass distribution, the effectiveness factor encodes the actuator and any added load, and the disturbance term encodes slopes, pushes, and hills. Simplicity here is a virtue, because it lets the comparison between controllers be read directly from the numbers rather than from modelling detail.

title: Added Load Case
body:
Added Load Case is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats added load case as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Adding a load to the balancing robot changes its physics: the same actuator torque now produces less angular acceleration, because it must move more mass, and the effective balance dynamics shift. A PID controller tuned for the unloaded robot therefore finds its gains effectively scaled down, and its response becomes slower and less accurate. The robot may still balance, since the reduced effective gains can remain near or above the stability threshold, but its tracking degrades in direct proportion to how much the load changed the plant.

The honest comparison has four entries, and its lesson is more careful than a simple adaptive victory. The nominal PID degrades under load; a PID retuned for the loaded plant, with gains scaled by the inverse of the effectiveness change, recovers fully, which proves that PID is capable of handling the load; an online neural learner improves on the degraded PID without any retuning, but in this model it recovers only part of the lost performance rather than matching the retuned PID. The adaptive advantage under load is therefore real but bounded: improvement without stopping, measuring, and retuning, plus, in the sweep record, rescue in the case where the fixed loop goes unstable outright. The demo runs all four cases side by side so the reader can see the degradation, the full recovery by retuning, and the partial recovery by learning, each measured rather than asserted.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for added load case. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. The output reads: PID nominal max deviation 0.12 rmse 0.0171 final tilt -0.0016; PID under load max deviation 0.12 rmse 0.0539 final tilt 0.01; PID retuned for load max deviation 0.12 rmse 0.0193 final tilt -0.002; neural learner under load max deviation 0.12 rmse 0.0492 final tilt 0.0087 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

In the demo the load is represented by an actuator-effectiveness factor of 0.35, meaning each unit of control torque has barely more than a third of its nominal effect, which pushes the fixed loop close to its stability boundary. The retuned PID scales its gains by the inverse of that factor, which is the correct response when the new plant is known. The neural learner keeps its original gains and adjusts one compensating weight online, in proportion to the measured error and the tilt. Comparing the root-mean-square error across the four rows shows the ordering the theory predicts: nominal best, loaded PID worst, retuned PID recovered, and the learner partway between the degraded and the retuned controller.

Moving onto a slope or hill changes the forces acting on the balancing robot rather than its mass: gravity now has a component along the slope that acts as a constant disturbance torque, pushing the robot persistently in one direction. The demo compares level ground, PID on a slope, and adaptive control on the same slope, so the transient penalty of waiting for the integral can be measured rather than asserted.

title: The Tuning Burden
body:
The Tuning Burden is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats the tuning burden as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

The tuning-burden argument is the structural core of the case for adaptation. If a PID controller must be tuned in advance for every environment it might meet, then the tuning task grows with the number of distinct environments, and that number grows combinatorially: every load level multiplies every slope, every friction value, and every mass, so a modest grid of five values in four dimensions is already hundreds of tuning sessions. Finer grids, more dimensions, and continuous rather than gridded variation push the count further, without any natural stopping point.

Online adaptation breaks this scaling by replacing advance enumeration with runtime estimation. Instead of visiting every combination before deployment, the controller estimates the combination it is actually in, while running, and the cost of that estimation does not grow with the number of combinations that might have occurred. This is a structural advantage, not a claim that adaptation is free: estimation takes time, can be wrong, and must itself be kept stable, as the stability record discusses. The demo computes the coarse-grid count and its tuning time, then shows how a fine grid of ten values per dimension reaches ten thousand combinations, to make the combinatorial growth concrete.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for the tuning burden. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. The argument does not depend on the exact figure: whatever the per-tune cost, it is multiplied by the number of combinations, while the adaptive controller's runtime estimation cost is paid once per deployment rather than once per combination. title: Stability Guarantees
body:
Stability Guarantees is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats stability guarantees as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Stability is where PID's maturity shows most clearly. For the linearised balancing model, stability reduces to two inequalities that can be checked by inspection: the proportional gain must exceed the gravity overturning term, and the total damping must be positive. A Lyapunov function, an energy-like quantity built from the tilt and the angular rate, can be shown to decrease along every trajectory when those inequalities hold, which proves that the robot returns to upright from any small disturbance. That proof is short, general, and independent of the particular trajectory, which is why PID remains the default wherever a stability argument must be shown to a reviewer or a regulator.

Learned and adaptive controllers do not yet enjoy the same simplicity. Their stability arguments must cover the learning loop as well as the control loop, must bound the estimator's error, and must often hold only within a region of the state space or under assumptions about how fast the plant changes. Research in this area is active and real, including Lyapunov-based adaptive laws and verified neural controllers, but the arguments are longer, narrower, and harder to audit than the PID proof. The demo traces the PID Lyapunov function over one hundred steps, showing it shrinking as the robot settles, and prints the two stability margins for inspection.

title: When PID Is the Right Choice
body:
When PID Is the Right Choice is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats when pid is the right choice as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

PID is the right choice when the plant is stable, well characterised, and operated within the conditions it was tuned for. Fixed industrial processes, laboratory rigs, and robots whose load and environment vary little all fit this description, and in those settings PID offers deterministic behaviour, a short stability proof, negligible compute cost, and a tuning procedure that any controls engineer can audit. Its weakness under change is simply not exercised when change is absent or small.

PID is also the right choice when the deployment demands formal review or approval, or long unattended operation under a fixed specification. A controller whose behaviour can be derived from three numbers and a plant model is easier to test exhaustively, easier to explain to a non-specialist reviewer, and easier to bound in its worst case than a controller whose behaviour depends on learned weights and an online estimator. The demo scores PID across five criteria, giving it high marks where it earns them and a low mark for adaptation under change, which is the honest shape of its profile.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand-typed claim. title: When Adaptive Control Is the Right Choice
body:
When Adaptive Control Is the Right Choice is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats when adaptive control is the right choice as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Adaptive control is the right choice when the plant changes during operation, when the deployment environment cannot be enumerated in advance, or when the cost of stopping to retune exceeds the cost of carrying an estimator. Field robots, robots that pick up and put down varied loads, and systems that must keep working through damage or wear all fit this description. In those settings the adaptive controller's ability to estimate the present plant while running is not a luxury but the only practical route to continued operation.

The choice carries real costs that must be budgeted. The stability argument is harder, the behaviour is less deterministic, the estimator needs monitoring for divergence, and a badly chosen learning rate can destabilise a loop that a fixed PID would have held. Adaptive control is therefore not a general replacement for PID but a tool for deployments where change is the dominant fact. The demo scores it across five criteria with the mirror image of the PID profile: high marks for adaptation and tuning burden, low marks for determinism and stability simplicity.

title: Hybrid Approaches
body:
Hybrid Approaches is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats hybrid approaches as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

Hybrid approaches refuse the forced choice between PID and learned control. The usual design keeps a tuned PID loop as the base controller, guaranteeing the stability margins and deterministic behaviour of the classical loop, and adds a learned compensator that estimates disturbances, unmodelled dynamics, or load changes and corrects for them. If the learned layer fails or is disabled, the system degrades to the PID loop rather than to uncontrolled fall, which is a safety property neither pure approach offers on its own.

The hybrid design also answers the stability objection in a practical way. The base loop's Lyapunov argument continues to hold for the nominal plant, and the learned layer can be bounded, rate-limited, or supervised so that its contribution cannot overturn the base loop's margins. What is given up is some of the pure adaptive controller's freedom, since the learned layer operates within limits set by the base loop, but what is gained is deployability in settings where a pure learned controller could not yet be approved. The demo runs a combined load-plus-slope case with PID alone and with the hybrid, showing the compensation layer recovering performance the base loop loses.

dt = 0.02
def run(Kp, Ki, Kd, load=1.0, dist=0.0, adapt=0.0):
    theta = 0.12; omega = 0.0; integ = 0.0; prev = 0.0; dhat = 0.0
    maxdev = 0.12; sse = 0.0
    for i in range(500):
        err = -theta
        integ += err * dt
        deriv = (err - prev) / dt; prev = err
        u = Kp * err + Ki * integ + Kd * deriv
        if adapt:
            dhat += -adapt * err * dt; u -= dhat
        u = max(-12.0, min(12.0, u))
        omega += (9.81 * theta + u * load - 0.4 * omega + dist) * dt
        theta += omega * dt
        maxdev = max(maxdev, abs(theta)); sse += err * err
    import math
    return maxdev, math.sqrt(sse / 500.0), theta

def run_neural(Kp, Ki, Kd, load=1.0, dist=0.0, lr=50.0):
    theta = 0.12; omega = 0.0; integ = 0.0; prev = 0.0; w = 0.0
    maxdev = 0.12; sse = 0.0
    for i in range(500):
        err = -theta
        integ += err * dt
        deriv = (err - prev) / dt; prev = err
        u = Kp * err + Ki * integ + Kd * deriv + w * theta
        w += lr * err * theta * dt
        u = max(-12.0, min(12.0, u))
        omega += (9.81 * theta + u * load - 0.4 * omega + dist) * dt
        theta += omega * dt
        maxdev = max(maxdev, abs(theta)); sse += err * err
    import math
    return maxdev, math.sqrt(sse / 500.0), theta

title: Evaluation Methodology
body:
Evaluation Methodology is a record in the PID Neural Network Control Database. PID control versus neural-network control for a balancing robot, compared fairly: both balance at baseline, and the comparison is about adaptability under change. It treats evaluation methodology as a checkable unit of work: the inputs are stated plainly, the method is applied step by step, the result is recorded, and the checks are listed so that another reader can repeat the work and reach the same result.

A fair comparison between PID and adaptive control must be designed before it is run, or it will favour whichever controller its author prefers. The protocol used across this database has five rules: both controllers face identical conditions, including identical initial tilts and disturbance sequences; several metrics are reported together, because any single metric can hide a weakness; the comparison covers baseline conditions as well as changed conditions, so baseline competence is never confused with adaptability; tuning effort is reported as a cost, including retuning time for the PID entries; and failure is defined in advance by a deviation threshold, so that a controller cannot be rescued after the fact by redefining success.

Metrics matter because they measure different things. Root-mean-square error summarises the whole run, maximum deviation captures the worst moment, settling step measures how long recovery takes, and final error shows where the controller ends up. A controller can win on final error while losing badly on the transient, as the slope record shows, so reporting one metric alone would mislead. The demo computes all four metrics for one fixed settling trace, showing the arithmetic behind each and the requirement that they be reported together.
